public_rationale: The October 1, 2024 research describes predictable capability scaling and differences in training efficiency across model families, but does not establish declining frontier capability gains per proportional resource increase [e1]. Reuters reported pretraining plateau concerns on November 12, 2024, after the November 9 cutoff; the reported experiments lack resource-normalized measurements and precise dates [e2]. Neither item establishes whether useful returns from scaling diminished during January 1–November 9, 2024 [e1, e2].
limitations: The evidence lacks a comparable series of frontier training runs measuring capability gains against proportional increases in compute and data [e1, e2].
The reported private experiments do not separate scaling effects from other training changes [e2].
Predictable capability improvement alone does not establish whether marginal returns increased or decreased [e1].

our_interpretation: Read diminishing returns as smaller useful capability improvements from comparable proportional increases in pretraining scale.
The April reference identifies an earlier assertion; the present-tense claim describes the state by November 9.
Use calendar 2024 through publication as the latest development period indicated by the context, with older generations as baselines.
Distinguish a practical slowdown in capabilities from the mathematical curvature of prediction-loss scaling.
criteria.support_condition: Consistent evaluations and resource measurements establish that successive frontier scaling increases yielded smaller useful capability gains during the target period.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable evaluations establish sustained or increasing useful capability gains for comparable scaling increases across the relevant frontier generations.
